seoTitle: Rent vs. Buy VDS — When Each Model Makes Financial Sense
metaDescription: Renting a VDS trailer at $1,500-$2,200/mo is opex with no hardware risk. Purchase is capex with a 5-7 year depreciation curve. Here's how to decide.
heroEyebrow: Two financial models for the same VDS hardware
heroSubhead: We rent. Most customers rent. Some customers buy. Here's the honest financial decision tree — when rental is correct, when purchase makes sense, and how the breakeven math actually works.
body:
## Why this comparison matters

VDS hardware is available two ways: monthly rental (the default and the most common) or outright purchase (less common, available for portfolios at a certain scale). The choice is a financial decision, not a product decision — the trailer, VMS, and SOC are identical either way. This page lays out when each shape is correct.

## The feature matrix

| Dimension | Monthly Rental | Outright Purchase |
|---|---|---|
| Monthly cost | $1,500-$2,200 all-in | $0 after purchase |
| Upfront cost | None | $45,000-$78,000 per unit |
| Hardware refresh | Included inside term | Customer responsibility after 5 years |
| Repair / replacement | Vendor-side (48-hour SLA) | Vendor-side under support contract |
| SOC included | Yes | Separate monthly per unit (~$800-$1,200) |
| VMS subscription | Yes | Separate monthly per unit (~$200-$400) |
| Cellular data | Yes | Customer pays carrier directly |
| Capex vs. opex | Opex | Capex (depreciation) |
| Procurement complexity | Low | Higher (PO, asset tagging) |
| Tax treatment | Deductible operating expense | Depreciable asset (5-7 yr) |
| Site portability | Easier (return at end) | Customer owns logistics |
| Best for | Projects 3-36 months, multi-site portfolios under 20 units | Stable 5+ year deployments, federal projects, fleets 20+ units |
| Break-even vs. rental | N/A | ~30 months at $2,200/mo |
| Termination flexibility | 30-90 day notice after term | Sell or store unit |

## When to rent

**Project-based work.** Construction projects, event security, seasonal coverage, temporary lots — rental is the right answer because you're not committing to a permanent asset for a temporary need.

**Multi-site portfolio under 20 units.** The administrative cost of capitalizing, asset-tagging, and tracking depreciation on 5-15 units rarely pays back vs. just renting. Rental keeps it on one MSA and one monthly invoice.

**Anyone who values opex over capex.** Site general conditions and security monthlies absorb rental easily. Capital budgets often don't.

**Anyone who wants hardware refresh included.** Our rental terms include hardware refresh — when we ship a new platform generation, your fleet rotates to it inside the rental term at no incremental cost. Purchase customers own a hardware vintage and decide when to upgrade.

**Anyone who doesn't want to own a depreciating asset.** Five years from now, you don't have to figure out the salvage value or storage of a rented unit.

## When to purchase

**Federal contracts with capitalization mandates.** Some federal programs (FEMA, DOE, certain DoD installations) require capital ownership of deployed infrastructure for compliance or accounting reasons. Purchase fits that model.

**Stable deployments expected to run 5+ years on the same site.** If you know with certainty a single unit will sit at the same site for 5+ years, the rental math is roughly $132,000 over 60 months vs. a purchase price plus support contract. The break-even math favors purchase at roughly month 30 of continuous deployment.

**Fleets of 20+ units in long-term programs.** At scale, customers with internal asset management teams sometimes prefer to own the fleet, capitalize it on the balance sheet, and contract VDS only for SOC + VMS + support.

**Specific tax positions.** Section 179 expensing or bonus depreciation may make a purchase year-one accounting attractive for some buyers. Talk to your tax advisor.

## Break-even math

For a single Sky Guard MSU at $2,200/mo rental vs. a $68,000 purchase + $1,000/mo combined SOC + VMS + support:

- **Rental cost at month 30:** $2,200 × 30 = $66,000
- **Purchase cost at month 30:** $68,000 + ($1,000 × 30) = $98,000
- **Rental wins through month 30, breakeven near month 32**, purchase pulls ahead at month 36+ assuming the hardware doesn't need replacement.

The big asterisk: hardware replacement cycle. Mobile surveillance hardware in a harsh outdoor environment has a 5-7 year useful life. At year 5 of ownership, you're spending $40,000-$60,000 to refresh. Rental customers get that refresh inside the term at no incremental cost. Adjust the math accordingly for any deployment beyond 60 months.

## Hybrid model — own some, rent some

Some larger customers run a hybrid fleet: purchase units for known-permanent sites, rent units for project-based or surge coverage. This works particularly well for utilities, municipalities, and large GCs running concurrent permanent and project deployments.

## How to think about it

Three questions:

1. **How long will this unit sit at one site?** Under 36 months: rent. 36-60 months: it's a coin flip, slightly favors rent. Over 60 months with stable site: consider purchase.

2. **How does your finance team prefer to book it?** If opex is preferred (most security budgets), rent. If your team has unused capex and wants to capitalize, purchase is available.

3. **Do you want to manage hardware lifecycle or have it managed for you?** Rental = managed. Purchase = your responsibility after support contract term.

faq.q: Can I convert a rental to a purchase mid-term?
faq.a: Yes. We offer a conversion path that credits a portion of rental payments against purchase price, typically up to 12 months of rental credit. Specific terms documented per deal.

faq.q: What's the resale value of a 5-year-old unit?
faq.a: Limited secondary market. Most purchased units stay in service with the original owner. We don't broker resale.

faq.q: Does purchase change the SOC pricing?
faq.a: The SOC service is separately priced for purchase customers at approximately $800-$1,200 per unit per month depending on the analytic stack and call volume.

faq.q: Are there minimum fleet sizes for purchase?
faq.a: We sell purchase contracts for fleets of 5+ units typically. Single-unit purchases are evaluated case-by-case.

faq.q: What about lease-to-own?
faq.a: Available on request. Effectively a structured rental with purchase trigger at month 48. Talk to procurement on the architecture call.

seoTitle: Solar vs. Diesel Mobile Surveillance — Power Source Compared
metaDescription: Diesel runs 7-14 days between refuels at $400-$900/mo. Solar runs indefinitely with no fuel, no emissions, no theft target
heroSubhead: Diesel generators run mobile surveillance for 7-14 days between refuels and cost $400-$900/month in fuel and service. Solar runs indefinitely with no fuel, no emissions, and no fuel-theft target. Here's where each power source wins.
body:
## Why this comparison matters

Mobile surveillance units need power. Two architectures dominate the market: solar-plus-battery and diesel generator. Some vendors offer hybrid. VDS deploys solar-plus-battery as standard with a generator backup option for specific high-latitude winter sites.

The choice is consequential. Solar wins on operating cost, environmental compliance, theft profile, and noise. Diesel wins on uptime certainty in extreme low-light conditions and on continuous load capacity. This page lays out the math and the failure modes.

## The feature matrix

| Dimension | Diesel Generator | Solar + Battery (VDS standard) |
|---|---|---|
| Continuous runtime between intervention | 7-14 days | Indefinite (in spec sun) |
| Fuel cost per month | $400-$900 | $0 |
| Refuel logistics required | Yes — fuel truck or jerry cans | None |
| Maintenance cost / mo | $100-$300 (oil, filters, service) | <$20 amortized |
| Emissions (CO2, NOx, particulates) | Yes, regulated in some jurisdictions | None |
| Noise | 60-75 dB at unit | Silent |
| Fuel theft risk | Real (especially rural/remote sites) | None |
| Cold-weather start reliability | Variable (needs block heater below 20°F) | N/A |
| Performance in week-long overcast | Excellent | Designed for 7-10 day zero-sun |
| Performance in Arctic winter (4 hr daylight) | Excellent | Marginal — generator backup recommended |
| Carbon-footprint reporting | Counted | Zero |
| Restricted-area permitting | Often requires emissions permit | Typically permit-free |
| Footprint | Generator + fuel tank | Solar array + battery pack |
| Failure mode | Out of fuel = dark | Battery deep discharge = recovery cycle |
| Site-up time | Faster (no panel deploy) | 4-6 hours including panel deploy |

## Where diesel wins

**Arctic and sub-Arctic winter sites.** At latitudes above 60° N, December has 4 hours of daylight or less. Even oversized solar arrays struggle. Diesel runs regardless.

**Industrial sites with extreme continuous load.** If the surveillance trailer is also powering ancillary equipment (heated enclosure, supplemental lighting, secondary radar) the load may exceed solar generation capacity even with full sun. Diesel handles continuous heavy load.

**Sites with existing fuel logistics.** A construction site that already has a fuel truck on a weekly schedule for heavy equipment has effectively zero marginal cost to add a generator to the rotation. The fuel logistics cost is sunk.

**Continuous deployment over 7+ days of zero sun.** Where weather modeling shows sustained heavy overcast (Pacific Northwest winter, Great Lakes lake-effect snow corridors), an oversized solar array works but adds cost and footprint. Diesel with backup solar is sometimes more efficient.

## Where solar wins (and is VDS standard)

**Operating cost.** Solar fuel cost is zero. Battery replacement cost amortizes to <$20/mo. Diesel fuel runs $400-$900/mo plus $100-$300/mo service. Over a 24-month deployment, solar saves $12,000-$28,000 per unit.

**No refuel logistics.** Diesel needs a refuel cycle — a truck or human visiting the site every 7-14 days. That's an operating burden, a logistics cost, and a security exposure (the refuel team has access to your site weekly). Solar units run themselves.

**No emissions.** California air resources regulations, certain federal site requirements, and an increasing number of municipal permits restrict or prohibit diesel generator operation. Solar units sidestep the entire compliance conversation.

**No fuel theft target.** Rural and remote construction sites report diesel fuel theft as a recurring problem — a thief siphoning the generator's tank during overnight. Solar units have no fuel to steal. The panels and batteries are physically integrated into the trailer and difficult to remove without specific tools.

**Silent operation.** Diesel generators at 60-75 dB are audible at 100+ feet. On urban infill sites, that noise generates neighbor complaints and sometimes municipal noise-ordinance citations. Solar units are silent.

**Zero carbon footprint.** For customers reporting Scope 1/Scope 2 emissions to investors, regulators, or sustainability frameworks, solar surveillance is reported as zero. Diesel is counted.

**VDS designs for 7-10 day zero-sun autonomy.** Our battery sizing assumes a worst-case dark week. We deploy in Seattle, Portland, Chicago, Buffalo, and across the Northeast year-round without weather-driven shutdowns.

## Cost math over 24 months — single mid-load site

- **Diesel:** $600/mo fuel + $200/mo service = $800/mo × 24 = **$19,200 in operating cost above the unit rental**, plus the refuel-logistics labor (typically 2-4 hours per refuel event × ~80 events = $4,000-$8,000 labor).
- **Solar (VDS standard):** $0 fuel, <$20/mo amortized battery wear = **<$480 operating cost**, no logistics labor.

Net solar savings: **$22,720-$26,720 over 24 months per unit.**

## Failure-mode comparison

**Diesel failure modes:**
- Out of fuel — unit goes dark within hours of empty tank
- Cold-start failure below 20°F without block heater
- Mechanical failure (alternator, starter, fuel pump)
- Fuel theft or contamination
- Refuel-truck no-show or weather-delayed access

**Solar failure modes:**
- Battery deep-discharge after >10 days zero sun (recovery cycle on next sunny day)
- Panel obscuration (heavy snow, debris) — requires manual clear
- MPPT controller failure (rare, vendor-replaced)
- Battery wear at 8-10 years of cycling

The solar failure mode is recoverable. The diesel failure modes generally require a truck roll.

## When to specify generator backup

For sites at high latitude with sustained sub-2-hour daylight in winter, or sites with sustained heavy load above solar generation capacity, we'll specify a generator backup. The default unit is solar-only because the default site doesn't need diesel and benefits from operating-cost savings.

## How to decide

Three questions:

1. **Where is the site?** Below 50° N latitude with normal cloud cover: solar always wins. Above 60° N in winter: generator or hybrid.

2. **What's the load?** Standard surveillance (cameras + LTE + analytics): solar handles it. Adding ancillary heavy loads (heated maintenance enclosure, supplemental floodlighting): may need diesel or hybrid.

3. **What's the permitting and reporting environment?** California, parts of the EU, federal sites with emissions reporting: solar removes friction. Industrial construction with existing fuel logistics: diesel is operationally fine.

faq.q: What if snow covers the solar panels?
faq.a: Our panels are angled for snow shedding. In heavy events, the SOC sees declining battery state-of-charge and notifies the customer for a manual clear if needed. Most events resolve on first sun.

faq.q: Can a thief steal the batteries?
faq.a: Battery packs are integrated into the trailer chassis, locked, and physically armored. We have zero documented battery theft incidents across 500+ deployments.

faq.q: What's the battery chemistry?
faq.a: LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate). Higher safety profile than NMC, longer cycle life (8-10 years), and tolerant of partial-state-of-charge operation.

faq.q: Is generator backup an additional cost?
faq.a: Yes, for the specific sites that need it. Most customers don't need it. We'll specify on the architecture call if your site is in a generator-recommended zone.

faq.q: Does solar work in winter on the East Coast?
faq.a: Yes — we have continuous winter deployments in Pennsylvania, New York, Massachusetts, and Maine. Battery sizing accounts for shorter daylight and overcast weeks.

finalCTABody: Send the site address and expected load. We'll come back with a sun-angle analysis, load model, and the right power configuration for your deployment.

seoTitle: VDS vs. Fixed Cameras — Mobile Solar vs. Wired Install
metaDescription: Fixed cameras need power, network, and 5-15 days of install lead time. A VDS trailer site-ups in 4-6 hours and moves when the site moves
heroSubhead: Fixed cameras are the right answer for permanent indoor and exterior installations with reliable power and network. They are the wrong answer for construction sites, lots, yards, and any perimeter that changes. VDS trailers site-up in 4-6 hours and redeploy when the site moves.
body:
## Why this comparison matters

Most security buyers default to "install fixed cameras" because that's how surveillance has been done for thirty years. Fixed cameras are the right answer for many use cases — a permanent office building, an interior production floor, a permanent loading dock. They are the wrong answer for any site where power, network, or geometry will change in the next 18 months.

The case for mobile solar surveillance comes down to three numbers: install lead time, total install cost including trenching and conduit, and redeployment cost when the site advances. This page lays out when each architecture is correct.

## The feature matrix

| Capability | Fixed Cameras | VDS (Solar Mobile) |
|---|---|---|
| Site-up time | 5-15 days typical | 4-6 hours |
| Trenching required | Yes (often) | No |
| Conduit required | Yes (often) | No |
| Electrician required | Yes | No |
| Network drop required | Yes (POE or coax) | No (private LTE) |
| Pole or building mount required | Yes | No (trailer-mounted) |
| Permit lead time | Variable, often weeks | None on private property |
| Cost per camera installed | $1,500-$4,500 | Included in $2,200/mo |
| Redeployment cost | Re-install fee per move | $0 (towed by customer or VDS) |
| Best for permanent indoor sites | Yes | No |
| Best for construction sites | No | Yes |
| Best for lots, yards, perimeters | Depends on infrastructure | Yes |
| Solar-autonomous | No | Yes |
| Includes 24/7 SOC | No (separate contract) | Yes |
| Includes audio talk-down | No (additional hardware) | Yes |
| Storage on-site or cloud | NVR or cloud separate | Cloud + edge |
| Capex vs. opex | Capex install + opex license | All opex |

## Where fixed cameras win

**Permanent installations.** If the building isn't moving and the lot isn't changing for the next ten years, fixed cameras are the right architecture. They cost less per-camera at scale (after the install hump is paid).

**Density.** You can put 40 fixed cameras inside a warehouse for less per-camera than 40 mobile units. Where you need very high camera density on a permanent footprint, fixed wins.

**Indoor environment.** Inside a building with steady power and HVAC, fixed cameras live longer and cost less to maintain. We don't sell indoor solutions — that's Verkada, Spot AI, Avigilon territory.

**Specific architectural integration.** Where cameras need to integrate with existing access control, fire alarm, or building automation systems via wired protocols, fixed installs are often required.

## Where VDS wins

**Site-up in hours, not days.** A construction site that needs surveillance tomorrow waits 5-15 days for a fixed camera install — permit, trench, conduit, electrician, network drop, mount, configure. By then, the site has been hit twice. A VDS trailer arrives on a truck, levels in 90 minutes, and is recording within 4 hours.

**No trenching, no conduit, no electrician.** A typical fixed install on a vacant lot involves coordinating an electrician for power, a low-voltage contractor for network, and possibly a permit for trenching. Total cost commonly runs $3,000-$8,000 per camera before you ever see a frame of video. A VDS Sky Guard trailer needs an empty pad of dirt and a clear sky.

**Redeployable when the site changes.** Construction sites move. A camera positioned over the foundation phase is in the wrong place by the time framing starts. With fixed cameras, you pay an installer to relocate. With a VDS trailer, you hook a truck to the tongue and tow it to the new position. Cost: zero, time: an hour.

**Solar-autonomous off-grid.** Most construction sites don't have permanent power. Most parking fields don't have a 120V outlet at the back corner. Most water utility yards don't have network at the fence line. We bring our own power and our own network. Fixed cameras can't operate where there's no infrastructure.

**One contract for hardware + VMS + SOC.** Fixed cameras typically come with a camera invoice, an install invoice, a network configuration invoice, a VMS subscription, and (separately) a monitoring contract. VDS is one monthly that includes all of it.

**No capex.** Fixed cameras hit the capex budget — meaning they get argued over in budget cycles and depreciated over 5-7 years. VDS is opex, charged to the site's monthly security budget without procurement battles.

## Cost and TCO over 36 months — perimeter coverage at a 5-acre site

- **Fixed cameras:** 8 cameras × $2,800 installed = $22,400 capex. NVR + storage $4,000 capex. VMS license $80/cam/mo × 8 × 36 = $23,040. Monitoring contract $600/mo × 36 = $21,600. Power/network $200/mo × 36 = $7,200. **Total 36-month: $78,240.** Redeployment if site changes: $1,500-$4,000 per move.
- **VDS Sky Guard MSU:** $2,200/mo × 36 = **$79,200.** Redeployment included.

At 36 months the prices are similar. The difference is risk: if your site changes once during that period, the fixed install loses by $1,500-$4,000+. If you have 5-15 day site-up gaps, the fixed install loses by whatever was stolen in those gaps.

## When to pick which

**Pick fixed cameras when:**
- Permanent indoor enterprise deployment
- Building has reliable power and network at every camera location
- Site geometry will not change in the next 5+ years
- High camera density (40+ cameras inside a footprint)
- Capex budget is available and depreciation works
- You have a procurement window of 30+ days for install

**Pick VDS when:**
- Site needs surveillance within a week
- Site has no power or no network at the perimeter
- Site geometry will change inside the next 24 months
- You want opex, not capex
- You want SOC, VMS, and hardware on one contract
- You want to avoid trenching, conduit, and electrician coordination

**Pick both when:**
- Indoor enterprise + outdoor perimeter at the same property — common.

## Switching from a planned fixed install

1. **Re-scope the urgent need.** Most projects scoped for fixed install can run VDS at the perimeter during the install lead time, then decide whether the fixed install is still needed.
2. **Pilot the trailer.** A single Sky Guard deployment for 90 days proves out coverage and cost.
3. **Decide on permanent architecture.** Many customers find the trailer becomes the permanent answer for outdoor perimeter and the fixed install scope shrinks to just the building interior.

faq.q: Can VDS feed into an existing fixed-camera VMS?
faq.a: Yes, via ONVIF export. Most major VMS platforms can ingest our streams. We can also reverse the flow — ingest your fixed cameras into our VMS and run our analytics across both.

faq.q: Is solar reliable in cloudy regions?
faq.a: Yes. Our solar-plus-battery configuration runs 7-10 days of zero-sun autonomy in spec. We deploy in Seattle, Portland, Chicago, and the Northeast year-round.

faq.q: What's the noise from a fixed install we're missing?
faq.a: Trenching across a paved lot to run conduit is the killer. We've seen quotes range $40-$200 per linear foot of asphalt cut and patch. VDS trailers eliminate all of it.

faq.q: Will VDS work for a permanent installation?
faq.a: Yes — many customers run VDS for years on the same site without redeployment. We're not strictly a temporary solution. The redeployability is a feature when you need it, not a requirement.

finalCTAHeading: Skip the install lead time on your next site
finalCTABody: If you've been quoted a fixed install and the timeline doesn't work, send the site address. We'll deliver a VDS trailer faster than the electrician arrives.

metaDescription: Flock had 67 cameras exposed without passwords in January 2026 and 30+ city contract cancellations since 2025. VDS is private-site, US-only AWS
heroEyebrow: Private security infrastructure vs. community ALPR
heroSubhead: Flock built a city-scale ALPR network and is currently dealing with 30+ city cancellations, a January 2026 breach that exposed 67 cameras to the open internet without passwords, and an April 2026 California class action. VDS is private-site, hardware-isolated, and audit-logged. Different tools, different risk profiles.
body:
## Why this comparison matters

Flock Safety and VDS are not the same product. Flock sells fixed ALPR cameras into cities, HOAs, and police networks. VDS sells mobile, solar-autonomous surveillance trailers into construction sites, logistics yards, and private commercial properties. The reason this comparison exists is that buyers — particularly municipalities and HOAs — increasingly ask whether the Flock model is appropriate at all, and what a private-site alternative looks like.

The short version: if you're a city council member, an HOA board, or a private property owner who has been pitched Flock and wants a non-Flock path, this page lays out the architectural and political differences clearly.

## The feature matrix

| Capability | Flock Safety | VDS |
|---|---|---|
| Primary use case | License plate reads for police/HOA | Private-site perimeter security |
| Camera type | Fixed pole-mounted ALPR | Mobile solar trailer, multi-sensor |
| Data sharing model | Multi-agency, cross-jurisdiction network | Single-customer, private |
| Public-internet exposure (Jan 2026) | 67 cameras exposed without passwords | Zero exposure events on record |
| Network architecture | Internet-connected by design | Private LTE / VPN, no public IP |
| Audit log | Roles-based, retention varies | Immutable 12-month |
| Data residency | Not exclusively US AWS | US-only AWS |
| FTC investigation calls | Yes — Sen. Wyden, Jan 2026 | None |
| City contract cancellations (2025-26) | 30+ | None |
| ACLU / EFF public campaigns | Active | None |
| Class action pending | Yes — California, April 2026 | None |
| 24/7 in-house SOC | No | Yes |
| Audio talk-down | No | Yes |
| LE dispatch with live video | No (post-event ALPR data) | Yes |
| NDAA Section 889 compliant | Mixed reporting | Yes |
| Authorized for federal sites | Limited | NDAA-compliant deployments |

## Where Flock wins

**ALPR is a real capability.** If your specific need is reading license plates at scale and matching them against a hot list, Flock has the densest network in the country. We do not sell ALPR as a primary product. If you need 5,000 plate reads per hour at a city entry point, Flock does that and we don't.

**Speed of deployment in a friendly municipality.** Where city government is on board, Flock's pole installs are fast. Days, not weeks.

**Crime-tip workflow with local PD.** Flock's police-facing portal is mature. Detectives can search plates across a regional network in seconds. That workflow is real and useful when it isn't abused.

## Where VDS wins

**No public-internet exposure.** In January 2026, security researchers reported that 67 Flock Condor cameras were accessible on the open internet without passwords. The story was covered by 404 Media, Marketplace, and 9News. One of the exposed cameras was pointed at children on a swingset. Sen. Ron Wyden called for an FTC investigation. VDS trailers are not addressable from the public internet — operator access is over private LTE and authenticated VPN, with MFA required on every session.

**No cross-agency data sharing.** Footage from a VDS trailer belongs to the VDS customer who rented it. Nothing is shared across jurisdictions, nothing is sold to a data broker, nothing flows into a regional law-enforcement search portal unless the customer explicitly subpoena-responds. A class action filed in California in April 2026 alleges that Flock illegally shares ALPR data across state lines in violation of state privacy laws. VDS architecture makes that mode of failure structurally impossible.

**30+ Flock contract cancellations since January 2025.** Bend OR (January 2026), Eugene OR, Springfield OR, Talent OR, Flagstaff AZ, Olympia WA, Mountlake Terrace WA, Redmond WA, Lynwood WA, Cambridge MA — all on public record. The pattern is sustained civic backlash, not a one-off. If you're a municipality looking at private-site security for a specific facility (motor pool, public works yard, water treatment plant), VDS sidesteps the entire civic-debate cycle because the trailer is on private city-owned property, not in the public right-of-way.

**24/7 in-house SOC with sub-60-second escalation.** Flock is a data-and-camera company. VDS includes an active monitoring layer with audio talk-down and live-video LE dispatch. Different shape entirely.

## Cost and TCO

Flock contracts run roughly $2,500-$3,000 per camera per year, multi-year commit, paid upfront annually. A 20-camera city deployment is $50,000-$60,000/year before installation. VDS Sky Guard rents at $2,200/mo all-in, no upfront, month-to-month after the initial 90-day term. Different model, different commitment shape.

## Switching from Flock (or migrating away after a council vote)

1. **Scope the cancellation.** If your city or HOA has voted to end its Flock contract, identify the cancellation effective date and the data-deletion clause. Flock contracts vary on whether collected data is purged on termination.
2. **Identify the actual security need under the ALPR.** Most Flock buyers were solving a perimeter or property crime problem, not specifically a plate-reading problem. We re-spec the same outcome using mobile units.
3. **Deploy VDS to the highest-risk property.** Typically motor pool, public works yard, water utility, or community pool/parking facility.
4. **Document the alternative for the next council meeting.** We supply a one-page comparison your council can put in the minutes.

faq.q: Is VDS hostile to law enforcement?
faq.a: No. We dispatch LE with live video on customer sites every week. The difference is consent and scope — our customer owns the site, owns the footage, and authorizes the dispatch. We don't run a regional plate-reader network shared across agencies.

faq.q: What happened with the 67 exposed Flock cameras?
faq.a: In January 2026, security researchers found 67 Flock Condor cameras accessible on the open internet without authentication. The reporting was published by 404 Media and picked up by Marketplace, 9News, and others. One camera was reportedly pointed at a residential swingset. Sen. Ron Wyden formally called for an FTC investigation.

faq.q: Has VDS ever had a comparable exposure?
faq.a: No public exposure incidents on record. Our network architecture (private LTE, no public IP, MFA-required operator access) makes the specific failure mode that hit Flock structurally hard to reproduce.

faq.q: Can VDS read license plates if we need that capability?
faq.a: Yes, ALPR is an available analytic on the platform. It's not our primary product line and we don't operate a multi-customer plate-sharing network. If ALPR is your primary need at scale, we'll tell you honestly whether we're the right fit.

faq.q: We're an HOA — is mobile surveillance even legal in our state?
faq.a: In every state we operate (30+), yes, when deployed on private property with appropriate signage. We supply a state-specific signage package and a model HOA notice for resident communications.

## Why this comparison matters

Pro-Vigil is one of the older names in managed remote video monitoring. They've built a real business on the "virtual guard" model — live operators watching customer-owned (or third-party-installed) cameras and intervening when something happens. They publish a 97% deterrence claim and a 24-second response time.

The structural challenge with the Pro-Vigil model is that the platform underneath the monitoring is not their own. Cameras come from various installers. Network connectivity depends on the site. Repair and uptime depend on whoever installed the gear. When a camera goes down, the customer is in the middle of a vendor triangle.

VDS owns the full stack — the trailer, the cameras inside it, the LTE radio, the VMS, the analytics, and the SOC operators. When something breaks, there's one number to call and one team to fix it. This page lays out where Pro-Vigil's model wins, where the integrated approach wins, and what real customers report in public reviews.

| Capability | Pro-Vigil | VDS |
|---|---|---|

## Where Pro-Vigil wins

**Long-established virtual guard operation.** Pro-Vigil has been running live remote monitoring for two decades. The operational playbook for talk-downs and dispatch is mature.

**Works on existing camera estates.** If you've already paid for fixed cameras and just need a monitoring layer on top, Pro-Vigil's service-on-other-people's-hardware model fits. We can do that too via ONVIF ingest, but Pro-Vigil's commercial motion is built around it.

**Brand familiarity in commercial real estate.** Property managers know the name. If your procurement office wants a name they recognize for the monitoring line item, Pro-Vigil clears that bar.

## Where VDS wins

**One throat to choke when something breaks.** Public BBB complaints flag repair delays on Pro-Vigil deployments — including a documented case of a non-working camera taking over a week to repair because the installer and Pro-Vigil were each waiting on the other. With VDS, there is no installer middleman. Our truck, our trailer, our techs, our 48-hour onsite SLA.

**Hardware refreshed inside the rental term.** Glassdoor reviews from Pro-Vigil employees flag outdated technology in the field. With a service-layer model, you're stuck with whatever hardware the installer put in two or five years ago. VDS rotates hardware on a documented refresh cycle at no incremental cost.

**Documented escalation pipeline.** Pro-Vigil publishes a 24-second response time. We don't dispute it — but we want to be precise about what's being measured. Our published metric is <60 seconds from analytic trigger to operator action with live LE dispatch initiated. Our 97% number is false-alarm reduction (the percentage of analytic alerts our operators suppress before they ever reach the customer), not deterrence — a measurable operational metric, not a vendor-friendly outcome claim.

**SOC operator stability.** We're a Maryland operation with documented SOC operator tenure. Pro-Vigil's Glassdoor reviews indicate high turnover, which matters because consistent operators learn your specific sites, your access protocols, and your local PD relationships.

**Mobile and outdoor coverage.** Pro-Vigil doesn't sell solar-autonomous trailers. If your site has no power or moves quarterly, that's a non-starter for the Pro-Vigil model.

## Cost and TCO

Pro-Vigil monthly monitoring runs roughly $300-$800 per site for service only — but that excludes camera hardware, installation, network, and ongoing repair, which the customer pays separately. Real all-in cost lands $1,200-$2,500/mo depending on installer markup.

## Why this comparison matters

Physical security guards are the default at most construction sites, logistics yards, and commercial properties because they're the default. Procurement understands the line item, the project manager has used the same guard company for ten years, and "we should add a guard" is the answer to most perimeter problems.

The math has changed. Wages have risen sharply since 2022. Insurance costs for guard companies have risen. Coverage gaps from sleeping-on-shift incidents are documented in court records. And the alternative — solar-autonomous surveillance with a 24/7 SOC running audio talk-down — is now cheap, deployable in hours, and produces video evidence that wins criminal cases and insurance claims.

This page is the math, the documented case study, and the honest answer about where guards still win.

| Capability | 24/7 Guard FTE Coverage | VDS Sky Guard MSU |
|---|---|---|
| Annual cost (2026) | $60,000-$110,000 per FTE | $26,400 ($2,200/mo) |

| Detection in adverse weather | Variable | IR + thermal + 24/7 power |
| Annual turnover (industry avg) | 100-300% | SOC team measured in years |

## Where guards still win

**Physical intervention.** A trailer cannot tackle someone. If your specific risk profile requires physical intervention at the scene before law enforcement arrives, you need a human. We dispatch LE with live video in under 60 seconds — but a human guard already on-site is faster than a police response.

**Customer-facing service.** At a hotel, a country club, a high-end retail entrance, the uniformed presence is part of the brand. Guards do customer service work cameras can't.

**Specific access-control scenarios.** Manned gates with vehicle inspection, badge checks, package screening — these are guard tasks. VDS handles passive monitoring; guards handle active gatekeeping.

**Sites with persistent active threat.** Some sites — high-value cash handling, certain federal facilities, executive protection — require armed human presence. Our trailers don't replace that.

## Where VDS wins

**The cost math is brutal.** 24/7 guard coverage at a single site requires 3-4 FTEs (three 8-hour shifts plus overlap and PTO coverage). At a $20-$26/hr fully-loaded rate including benefits and overhead, that's $180,000-$440,000/year for one site. A Sky Guard MSU covers the same perimeter at $26,400/year. The savings recover the cost of a security director's salary on a single property.

**Documented ROI on a real project.** On a $28M Mid-Atlantic general contractor project, we replaced a guard contract running $32,400/mo with a single trailer at $4,000/mo (all-in including SOC). Result: 73% theft reduction, $0 insurance claims for the project duration, $340,800 saved in 12 months. We'll share the project name under NDA on the architecture call.

**No sleeping-on-shift risk.** Guard industry turnover runs 100-300% annually. Sleeping-on-shift is documented in court records and insurance claim disputes industry-wide. Our SOC operates from a single Maryland facility with W-2 employees on tenure. Roll call is logged. Operator activity is logged. Footage of the operator's screen is auditable on request.

**Video evidence wins criminal and civil cases.** When something happens at a guarded site, what often exists is the guard's incident report — a paper document with a narrative. When something happens at a VDS site, what exists is time-stamped HD video of the event with a recorded audio talk-down by the operator and a logged LE dispatch. Prosecutors prefer video. Insurance adjusters prefer video.

**Audio talk-down deters before LE arrives.** The moment an analytic fires, our operator can speak through the trailer's amplified speaker: "You are being recorded by Vision Detection Systems Security Operations Center. Police have been dispatched. Leave the property immediately." Documented intrusion rate drops sharply at first contact. Guards do this in person; we do it remotely and consistently.

**Scales sub-linearly across sites.** A 10-site portfolio needs 10 trailers and the same SOC. A 10-site guarded portfolio needs 30-40 FTEs. The cost curve diverges hard above 3 sites.

## Cost and TCO over 12 months — single mid-risk site

- **Guard coverage 24/7:** 3.5 FTE × $24/hr × 2,080 hrs = $174,720 base. Add 22% benefits + overhead = **$213,158/year**.
- **VDS Sky Guard MSU:** $2,200/mo × 12 = **$26,400/year**.

Difference: **$186,758/year**, with documented video evidence and zero shift-gap risk on the VDS side.

## Switching from guards to VDS

1. **Risk audit week 1.** We walk the site with your operations lead and identify which guard functions are passive monitoring (replaceable) and which are active intervention (retained).
2. **Pilot week 2-3.** A single Sky Guard MSU deploys to the highest-risk zone. Guard coverage continues in parallel. Both teams document incidents for comparison.
3. **Reduction week 4-6.** Guard hours reduce on a documented schedule. Most customers retain 1 shift of physical presence (often day-shift gate) and shift overnight coverage entirely to VDS.
4. **Quarterly review.** Cost savings reported back; coverage gaps (if any) identified and remediated.

## Why this comparison matters

| Capability | Spot AI | VDS |

## Where Spot AI wins

**Best-designed UI in the category.** No qualifiers needed. Spot AI's web app, mobile app, and AI-search experience are best-in-class for indoor video AI. If your team's primary daily tool is a search bar over video, Spot AI is the most pleasant tool in the market.

**G2 4.8/5 is the real deal.** 73 reviews at that rating is a serious signal. Spot AI customers genuinely like the product, and customer love compounds in B2B.

**Hybrid NVR plus cloud architecture.** For high-camera-count indoor sites where pure-cloud bandwidth is prohibitive, the hybrid model is well-engineered.

**Indoor AI analytics.** Person, vehicle, dwell, count, queue — the indoor analytics catalog is mature and the AI-driven search ("show me everyone wearing a red shirt who walked into receiving after 10pm") works.

## Where VDS wins

**We sell outdoor hardware. They don't.** Solar-autonomous trailers, mobile redeployment, off-grid power. If your perimeter, parking field, yard, lot, or construction site needs surveillance, Spot AI literally doesn't make a product for that. We do.

**24/7 in-house SOC included.** Spot AI is a software product. You watch the cameras (or your guard service does). VDS includes a Pikesville, Maryland-staffed SOC with sub-60-second escalation, audio talk-down, and LE dispatch with live video. Those are operations Spot AI is structurally not in.

**Direct sales for first deployment.** Spot AI is pivoting to 100% channel in 2026. Channel can be a good thing — local integrator support — but for the first deployment at a complex site, you may want a direct engineering call with the platform vendor. We support direct, especially for first deployments.

**NVR-reliability flags from public reviews.** Even with the strong overall G2 rating, several Spot AI reviews flag NVR hardware reliability — units failing, replacement timelines. VDS trailers don't have an NVR — recording is cloud-first with edge caching, so a single-component hardware failure doesn't take down a site's recording.

**Coexistence pattern that works.** Multiple VDS customers run Spot AI indoor and VDS outdoor on the same security team's pane of glass. If you're a Spot AI customer with an outdoor gap, we slot in cleanly without ripping anything out.

## Cost and TCO

Spot AI pricing is quote-based and varies by camera count and feature tier; typical mid-size deployments report $50-$120 per camera per month. NVR hardware is roughly $2,000-$5,000 per site, customer-purchased.

VDS Sky Guard at $2,200/mo includes the trailer, the cameras, the cloud storage, the SOC, the audio talk-down, the LE dispatch workflow, and hardware refresh inside the rental term. No per-camera license escalator.

For pure indoor 60-camera enterprise: Spot AI is often the right answer.
For pure outdoor mobile: VDS is the right answer and Spot AI doesn't offer the product.
For hybrid (indoor + outdoor): run both.

1. **Audit indoor vs. outdoor.** Most sites have a clear split. Indoor cameras stay on Spot AI; outdoor coverage moves to VDS Sky Guard.
2. **Define the operations split.** Spot AI users search and review indoor footage themselves. VDS SOC handles outdoor monitoring, audio talk-down, and LE dispatch.

In 2024-2025, Stealth Monitoring, ECAMSECURE, and GardaWorld merged into what is now ECAM. The combined entity monitors 140,000+ cameras daily and is the largest live remote monitoring service in North America. By any volume measure, ECAM is the biggest player in remote video monitoring.

The strategic question for buyers is whether scale equals fit. ECAM is a service company without first-party platform IP — they monitor cameras others install on platforms others built. The GardaWorld parentage adds a guard-services upsell motion that some customers want and others actively want to avoid. And the brand churn (Stealth → ECAMSECURE → ECAM in 18 months) creates real operational friction for procurement, signage, and customer-facing communications.

VDS is a smaller, more focused operation. We own the hardware, the VMS, the analytics, and the SOC under one brand we've operated since 2017. This page is for buyers deciding between scale and integration.

## The feature matrix

| Capability | Stealth / ECAM | VDS |
|---|---|---|
| Cameras monitored daily | 140,000+ | Customer-private |
| Years under current brand | <2 (ECAM since 2025) | 8 (VDS since 2017) |
| First-party hardware | No | Yes |
| First-party VMS | Limited | Yes |
| In-house 24/7 SOC | Yes | Yes |
| Mobile/solar trailers | No (rebrand may add) | Yes |
| Audio talk-down | Yes | Yes |
| LE dispatch with live video | Yes | Yes |
| Parent company | GardaWorld | Independent |
| Guard services upsell pressure | Yes | None |
| Single MSA for site | Multi-vendor | Single |
| Brand identity since 2024 | Stealth → ECAMSECURE → ECAM | VDS, unchanged |
| US-only AWS data residency | Not published | Yes |
| NDAA Section 889 | Variable by installer | Yes |
| 12-month immutable audit log | Variable | Yes |
| Documented escalation SLA | Published response time | <60 seconds escalation |
| False alarm reduction | Not published | 97% |

## Where Stealth / ECAM wins

**Scale of monitoring volume.** 140,000+ cameras monitored daily means deep operational pattern recognition. If you want a vendor that's seen every type of perimeter event a thousand times before, ECAM has the volume.

**Case study library across the merged entities.** Stealth, ECAMSECURE, and GardaWorld each brought multi-vertical references. The combined library is genuinely broad — retail, multi-family, construction, education, healthcare.

**Bundled guard services if you want them.** GardaWorld is one of the largest physical guard companies in the world. If you want a single vendor for both remote monitoring and physical patrols, the bundled offering is real.

## Where VDS wins

**Operational stability since 2017.** VDS has been one company under one brand since 2017. ECAM has had three brand identities in 18 months. That matters for site signage (which has to be updated each time), incident reports, customer-facing communications, and procurement file maintenance. Our customers don't have to update anything when their security vendor renames itself.

**First-party platform IP.** ECAM is a service layered on third-party cameras and third-party platforms. When a platform vendor changes pricing or sunsets a feature, ECAM and the customer are along for the ride. We own our platform end-to-end. Pricing and feature roadmap are decisions we make for our customers, not decisions made for us.

**No guard-services upsell pressure.** GardaWorld's commercial model points naturally toward "let's add physical guards." That's a legitimate service line, but customers regularly tell us they want the technology layer specifically because they're trying to reduce guard spend. With VDS, the conversation about guards never happens because we don't sell them.

**Mobile and solar hardware.** ECAM monitors fixed installations. No solar-autonomous trailers. If your need is mobile or off-grid, the entire ECAM proposition doesn't fit.

**Documented false-alarm metric.** We publish 97% false-alarm reduction as an auditable operational number — the percentage of analytic triggers our operators filter before they reach the customer. ECAM publishes response times but not false-alarm-suppression rates, which is the more operationally meaningful metric for security directors evaluating alert fatigue.

## Cost and TCO

ECAM monitoring runs $400-$1,200 per site per month for service only. Hardware and installation are separate, typically through an authorized integrator network with their own markups. All-in monthlies often land $1,400-$2,800/mo per site for fixed coverage, plus capex on the camera installation.

VDS Sky Guard at $2,200/mo includes the trailer, every camera on it, the LTE, the VMS, the SOC, the audio talk-down, and the LE dispatch workflow. No installer line item.

## Switching from Stealth / ECAM

1. **Identify the multi-vendor stack.** ECAM monitoring contract, separate installer maintenance contract, separate platform license. Map all three.
2. **Replace the stack with one VDS contract.** Sky Guard for mobile/perimeter coverage, ONVIF ingest where you want to keep existing fixed cameras.
3. **Brand-update the signage.** If your site signage references Stealth or ECAMSECURE, update to VDS — and don't expect to do it again soon, because we've kept one brand since 2017.
4. **Single quarterly review.** One contact, one report, one number to call.

faq.q: Is 140,000+ cameras monitored a meaningful operational advantage?
faq.a: Volume helps with pattern recognition in operator training. It doesn't substitute for first-party platform engineering. Our operators see fewer cameras than ECAM's, but every camera they see runs on the same VMS we built and the same analytics we tune.

faq.q: Why does the brand churn matter?
faq.a: Practically: site signage needs updating each rename. Procurement files need rebadging. Customer-facing letterhead and incident reports need new logos. Each rename is 2-6 hours of customer-side admin work that VDS customers never have to do.

faq.q: Does GardaWorld parentage actually pressure customers toward guard services?
faq.a: From customer reports, yes — quarterly business reviews often include guard service proposals. That may be useful for some buyers. For buyers specifically trying to reduce guard spend, it's noise.

faq.q: Can VDS scale to a 500-site portfolio?
faq.a: We currently run 500+ deployments across 30+ states. For 500-site portfolio rollouts, we run a dedicated account team and a documented multi-site SLA. References on the architecture call.

heroSubhead: Verkada has the best mobile app in the category — we'll say that on the record. They also had 150,000+ cameras hacked in 2021 and paid the largest CAN-SPAM settlement in FTC history in 2024. VDS is open hardware, US-only AWS, SOC-backed, no fake reviews on file.
body:
## Why this comparison matters

Verkada is the most polished enterprise cloud video product in the market. The mobile app is genuinely excellent. The unified access-plus-video story closes deals against Lenel and Genetec every week. We are not going to pretend otherwise.

We are also going to point out that Verkada was breached in March 2021 (150,000+ cameras, intruder accessed live feeds at psychiatric hospitals, women's health clinics, Tesla factories, and jails), paid $2.95M to the FTC in August 2024 (the largest CAN-SPAM penalty ever assessed), and was cited by the FTC for posting fake employee-written reviews. Those facts are public and they matter when you're picking the company that holds your video.

This page covers where Verkada genuinely wins, where VDS wins, and the architectural differences that matter for risk-sensitive buyers.

## The feature matrix

| Capability | Verkada | VDS |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile app UX (subjective) | Best in category | Functional, improving |
| Camera-agnostic VMS | No (Verkada cameras only) | Yes (ONVIF) |
| Hardware lock-in | Yes | No |
| Solar-autonomous outdoor unit | No | Yes |
| Indoor fixed camera line | Broad (dome, fisheye, multi-sensor) | Through partner OEMs |
| Access control integration | Native (Verkada AC) | Via integration |
| Cloud license cost / camera / year | $199-$1,799 | Included in monthly hardware rental |
| 24/7 in-house SOC | No | Yes |
| Audio talk-down | Limited (one-way audio on select models) | Yes, on every trailer |
| Major breach incident | March 2021 (150K+ cameras) | None on record |
| FTC settlement | $2.95M, August 2024 | None |
| Fake review citation by FTC | Yes (2024 case) | None |
| US-only AWS data residency | Mixed | Yes |
| NDAA Section 889 | Yes | Yes |
| Audit log retention | Variable by tier | Immutable 12-month |
| Integration breadth | Wide (Slack, Teams, etc.) | Focused (LE dispatch, BI tools) |
| Best fit | Corporate offices, indoor enterprise | Outdoor, mobile, perimeter |

## Where Verkada wins

**Best UX in the category, period.** The mobile app, the web console, the floor-plan view, the search experience — all genuinely well-designed. If your security director's primary daily tool is the mobile app on her phone, Verkada is hard to beat on user experience.

**Unified access and video.** Verkada Access (door controllers, badge readers) talks to Verkada Video in one console. If you're standing up a new corporate HQ and want one vendor for both, that's a real advantage and we don't match it natively.

**Indoor product line breadth.** Domes, fisheyes, multi-sensors, mini-domes, license-plate cameras, environmental sensors, alarm panels — Verkada has more SKUs than we do. For an indoor enterprise rollout, that catalog matters.

## Where VDS wins

**Camera-agnostic VMS.** Our platform accepts any ONVIF-compliant camera. Axis, Hanwha, Bosch, Avigilon, your existing fleet — we ingest the stream and run our analytics on top. Verkada's platform only runs Verkada cameras. If you already own $400K of cameras, that matters.

**Outdoor and mobile.** Verkada has no solar-autonomous outdoor trailer. We do — Sky Guard MSU, Swift Deploy, and Boundary Guard Pro, all assembled in Pikesville MD. If your security perimeter includes a construction site, a parking field, a yard, a remote substation, or a job site without power, we cover it and Verkada doesn't.

**24/7 in-house SOC.** Verkada is a software-plus-camera company. Monitoring is on you or your guard provider. VDS includes a Pikesville, Maryland-staffed SOC with <60-second escalation, 97% false-alarm reduction, audio talk-down on every trailer, and LE dispatch with live video pushed to the responding officer.

**Pricing transparency.** Verkada's cloud licenses run $199-$1,799 per camera per year, tiered opaquely. Customers regularly report sticker shock at renewal. VDS rolls everything — hardware, VMS, storage, SOC — into one monthly per unit. No per-camera license escalator at renewal.

**No breach or FTC settlement on the record.** The 2021 Verkada breach (Bloomberg, March 2021) exposed live feeds from psychiatric hospitals, women's health clinics, Tesla factories, and jails. The 2024 FTC settlement was $2.95M — the largest CAN-SPAM penalty in FTC history — and the case file specifically cited Verkada for posting fake reviews written by employees. We have zero comparable incidents on file.

## Cost and TCO over 36 months (24-camera enterprise site)

- **Verkada:** ~$15,000 hardware avg + ~$799/camera/yr license × 24 × 3 = $57,528 license + $15,000 = **$72,528** (hardware-low estimate; real-world deployments often run higher with multi-tier licensing).
- **VDS equivalent outdoor coverage:** 2 Sky Guard MSU at $2,200/mo × 36 = **$158,400** if you actually need mobile/outdoor — but if it's purely indoor enterprise, Verkada is the right tool. This is not always our deal.

We will tell you when Verkada is the right answer. For pure indoor corporate, it often is. For anything with an outdoor or mobile component, VDS wins on TCO and operational fit.

## Switching from Verkada (or running both)

1. **Audit your camera estate.** If you're 80% indoor enterprise and 20% perimeter/outdoor, the right architecture is often Verkada indoor + VDS outdoor. Both feed your security team.
2. **Re-license decision.** If your Verkada licenses renew in <12 months and you have an outdoor gap, we can rent units to bridge.
3. **Integrate, don't rip.** Our platform can ingest a Verkada RTSP stream where the customer has the export configured. Many customers run hybrid for 18-24 months before deciding to consolidate.

faq.q: Is the 2021 Verkada breach still relevant in 2026?
faq.a: The breach itself was March 2021. The FTC enforcement action concluded in August 2024 with a $2.95M settlement and specific findings about Verkada's security practices and fake-review postings. Both are part of the company's public security and ethics record as of today.

faq.q: Will VDS work alongside Verkada?
faq.a: Yes. We have multiple customers running Verkada indoor and VDS outdoor on the same security team's pane of glass. Our platform can ingest Verkada RTSP streams where the customer enables export.

faq.q: Why is Verkada's UX better?
faq.a: Honest answer: Verkada invested earlier and more heavily in product design and front-end engineering. They're roughly 1,500 employees vs. our 80. The gap is real and we're closing it, but if 2026 mobile app polish is decisive for you, factor it in.

faq.q: What does Verkada cost at renewal?
faq.a: Customers report 15-30% annual license escalators on renewal. Our monthly rental has no per-camera escalator inside the contract term.

finalCTABody: If you're a Verkada shop with an outdoor gap, send your site list. We'll come back with a hybrid coverage plan that protects your existing Verkada investment.
notes: Detail page. Treat Verkada with respect on UX — it's their real strength. Lean hard on the FTC settlement, breach, and outdoor/SOC gap.

## Where WCCTV wins

**Construction case study depth.** Turner Construction, LAX, IAH — public references on jobs of meaningful scale. If your GC's procurement office wants a name with documented airport work, WCCTV has the references.

**Simple rental model.** No software licensing tier conversation, no SOC sub-pricing — pay the monthly, get the trailer. The simplicity is real. We match it, but we'll give them credit.

**Established US ops despite UK origin.** They've been operating in the US long enough to have real American customer support, US service trucks, and US install capacity. They are not a UK-only company shipping units across the Atlantic.

## Where VDS wins

**Modern AI stack.** WCCTV's analytics platform is 2018-era. Modern construction sites need perimeter analytics, loitering detection, tailgate detection, and plate-reading running concurrently with low false-positive rates. Our 2026 stack delivers 97% false-alarm reduction in production deployments.

**US assembly, US data, US SOC.** We assemble trailers in Pikesville, Maryland. Our cloud runs on US-only AWS regions. Our SOC operators are W-2 employees in the United States. For federal-adjacent construction, government work, or critical infrastructure projects, the all-American supply chain matters at the procurement compliance layer.

**24/7 in-house SOC included.** WCCTV expects the customer (or the customer's monitoring vendor) to handle the human-in-the-loop layer. VDS includes the SOC in every monthly. Audio talk-down with operator escalation, LE dispatch with live video, documented sub-60-second escalation — all under one contract.

**NDAA Section 889 by default.** Every VDS deployment is NDAA Section 889 compliant. WCCTV's reporting on this is mixed and you need to verify per-deployment. For federal-adjacent work, that's a real operational difference.

**Documented construction ROI.** On a $28M Mid-Atlantic general contractor project, VDS reduced theft 73%, eliminated insurance claims, and cut security cost from $32,400/mo to $4,000/mo — saving $340,800 in 12 months. We can provide the project name under NDA on the architecture call.

## Cost and TCO

WCCTV quotes are not published; reported customer monthlies fall roughly in the $1,800-$2,800/mo range depending on configuration. VDS publishes its rates: Sky Guard $2,200/mo, Swift Deploy $1,500/mo, Boundary Guard Pro $1,800/mo, all-in with SOC and VMS included.

Over a 12-month project, the difference is rarely the headline monthly — it's the variability. WCCTV monthlies on long projects often drift upward at refresh. Our pricing is locked for the term.

## Switching from WCCTV

1. **Calendar the existing rental.** WCCTV contracts are typically month-to-month after the initial 90-day term. Identify your cancellation window.
2. **Schedule the swap.** Our delivery team coordinates with the WCCTV pickup so there's no coverage gap. Typical swap is a single day for a single-trailer site.
3. **Re-mount fixed assets where applicable.** Site signage and access protocols transfer; SOC liaison is assigned before the swap.
4. **Document the construction phases.** Our team plans trailer redeployment as the site advances — different positions for foundation, frame, finish, and close-out phases.

faq.q: Will VDS work on an airport or aviation project?
faq.a: Yes — we've deployed on aviation-adjacent construction. Federal site coordination requires advance review (FAA, TSA where applicable), which we handle on the procurement side.

faq.a: For federal-funded projects, FedRAMP-adjacent procurement requirements, and state contracts with data residency clauses, the answer to "where does the footage live" is a contract-eligibility question. US-only AWS gives a clean answer.

faq.q: Does WCCTV have an in-house SOC?
faq.a: Not in the United States in the same sense VDS does. They partner with third-party monitoring providers and expect customers to bring their own monitoring where required. We include it.

**Homes.** A single-family home does not need a solar-autonomous trailer. Deep Sentinel's fixed AI cameras with live agent monitoring are well-priced and well-designed for that buyer.

**Single storefronts and small businesses.** A coffee shop, a small office, a single-bay auto shop. The Deep Sentinel hub plus 2-4 cameras and a monthly plan is the right shape and the right budget.

**DIY install and short install timelines.** Deep Sentinel ships, you mount cameras, you go live in hours. No site survey, no trailer transport.

**Interactive AI talk-down at the consumer tier.** Deep Sentinel's interactive agents are a thoughtful product for residential use.

## Where VDS wins

**Sites without power.** Solar-autonomous units mean construction sites, undeveloped land, utility substations, and remote yards get full coverage without trenching or a generator.

**Sites that move.** Construction projects relocate the active work zone every few weeks. Lay-down yards shift. Mobile units redeploy in hours. Fixed cameras do not.

**Multi-acre and perimeter coverage.** A 20-acre lay-down yard, a 40-acre solar farm, or a quarter-mile substation perimeter is not a fixed-camera job. Mobile units with elevated masts, pan-tilt-zoom cameras, and AI-driven detection cover that footprint with fewer assets.

**Commercial governance.** NDAA Section 889 in writing. US-only AWS data residency. AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit. 12-month immutable audit log. RBAC and MFA. These are the answers a commercial security committee, an insurance underwriter, or a federal-flow-down GC needs.

- **You run a single small business storefront** — Deep Sentinel.
- **You are a GC, utility, municipal site manager, retail park operator, or multi-site enterprise** — VDS.
- **You need to move the cameras every few weeks** — VDS.
- **You have a site with no electrical service** — VDS.

h1: Manufacturer vs. Integrator — Buying Direct vs. Buying through Security 101
heroSubhead: Integrators like Security 101 resell multiple brands and assemble them into one system. Manufacturers like VDS design, build, monitor, and support a single product line end-to-end. Both models work. Here is how to know which one fits your program.
body:
## Why this comparison matters

Security 101 is the most-recognized national US integrator. They resell Verkada, Avigilon, Genetec, and others, and assemble those products into a system for the buyer. VDS is a manufacturer — we design and build mobile surveillance hardware (Sky Guard, Swift Deploy, Boundary Guard Pro), run the AI VisionStream platform, and operate a 24/7 US SOC under one roof.

Neither model is automatically better. The right model depends on what you are buying.

## The comparison matrix

| Criterion | VDS (Manufacturer-Direct) | Security 101 / Multi-Brand Integrator |
|---|---|---|
| Product breadth | One specialized product line — mobile surveillance | Many brands — cameras, access control, intrusion, intercom, fixed VMS |
| Single pane of glass across 10+ vendors | No — we are one vendor | Yes — integrator's strength |
| Hardware ownership | Yes — VDS designs and builds | No — resells third-party hardware |
| Pricing transparency | Published — from $1,500/mo, $38,000 purchase | Integrator margin layered on top of MSRP |
| Manufacturer support | Direct — engineer to engineer | Through integrator |
| Warranty owner | VDS | Varies by reseller terms |
| SOC ownership | VDS in-house US SOC | Outsourced or third-party referral |
| NDAA Section 889 traceability | Direct from manufacturer | Through reseller chain |
| Brand lock-in risk | Single-brand dedicated program | Whatever the integrator resells |
| Change-order flexibility | Direct line to engineering | Through integrator's process |
| Geographic install reach | VDS field service + integrator partners | Integrator's footprint |
| Right for heterogeneous building security | Not the right fit | Yes |
| Right for mobile-surveillance program | Yes — direct manufacturer | Add markup, lose direct line |

## Where an integrator like Security 101 wins

**Heterogeneous environments.** A corporate campus with badge access control, intercoms, fixed surveillance from two brands, intrusion panels, and a parking gate system needs an integrator. Stitching those products together is the integrator's job and they are good at it.

**One-throat-to-choke across 10+ vendors.** If your security director wants one PO, one trouble ticket address, and one annual review covering everything, the integrator is the model.

**Existing relationship.** If Security 101 already installed your access control and your fixed surveillance, adding the mobile surveillance trailer through them is sometimes simpler than starting a parallel relationship.

**Geographic install density.** National integrators have install techs in markets where a single manufacturer may not.

## Where buying direct from VDS wins

**Mobile surveillance is a dedicated program.** If you are spending $50,000+ per year on mobile surveillance trailers across multiple sites, you are running a dedicated program. Buying it through an integrator adds margin without adding value.

**Manufacturer SOC and warranty.** When a unit fails at 3 AM, you want the manufacturer's SOC and the manufacturer's field service. Going through an integrator means the integrator opens a ticket with VDS — extra step, no benefit.

**Transparent pricing.** Published rates: Swift Deploy from $1,500/mo, Boundary Guard Pro from $1,800/mo, Sky Guard from $2,200/mo, Sky Guard purchase from $38,000. An integrator quote layers margin on top of MSRP. You are paying for the relationship.

**NDAA Section 889 traceability.** When the GC's federal flow-down audit lands on your desk, you need a component bill of materials. Direct from manufacturer is one document. Through an integrator is two paper trails and a phone call.

**Direct engineering line.** Site-specific deployment questions get answered by the engineer who designed the unit, not by a sales rep who resells the unit.

## Pricing comparison

| What you pay | Direct from VDS | Through an integrator |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware MSRP | List | List |
| Integrator margin | $0 | 10–30% typically |
| Annual service | Published rate | Marked up |
| Change orders | Direct billing at engineering rate | Marked up |

Numbers vary by integrator and by deal size. Ask any integrator for the manufacturer's MSRP alongside the integrator quote. If they will not show it, that itself is information.

## A note on integrator partners

VDS works with security integrators through our /partners program. If you are an integrator reading this — we are not trying to cut you out. We are trying to be honest with end-buyers about when a manufacturer-direct purchase is the better answer. Where the integrator relationship adds real value (heterogeneous environments, multi-vendor stitching, geographic install reach), we partner. Where it adds only margin, we encourage direct.

## Decision framework

**Buy through an integrator if:**
- You are buying mobile surveillance as one piece of a broader multi-vendor security system.
- You have an existing integrator relationship and the marginal install volume is small.
- You want one PO covering access control, fixed cameras, intrusion, and mobile.

**Buy direct from VDS if:**
- Mobile surveillance is a dedicated program with its own budget line.
- You need manufacturer-direct SOC, warranty, and engineering support.
- You need NDAA Section 889 traceability in one document.
- Your security committee values published pricing and no margin layer.
- You want the engineer who built the unit on the call when something needs to change.

faq.q: Does VDS sell through Security 101?
faq.a: We have partner relationships with integrators including some Security 101 franchises through /partners. Direct sales are also available and often the better path for dedicated mobile surveillance programs.

faq.q: Is buying through an integrator always more expensive?
faq.a: Usually yes, because integrators layer margin on MSRP. The trade-off is consolidation across multiple vendors. If that consolidation has value to your program, the margin is worth it. If you are running a dedicated mobile surveillance program, it usually is not.

faq.q: Can I get VDS hardware from Verkada or Avigilon dealers?
faq.a: No. VDS hardware is sold by VDS direct or through approved /partners. Verkada and Avigilon do not resell our mobile surveillance hardware.

faq.q: What is in VDS' partner program?
faq.a: Integrator referrals, co-quoted opportunities, install support, and SOC integration into the integrator's existing operations. See /partners.

faq.q: Will VDS work alongside my existing integrator?
faq.a: Yes. We have closed deals where the integrator handles fixed surveillance and access control while VDS runs the mobile program directly. The integrator stays in the relationship; VDS owns the mobile piece end-to-end.

finalCTAHeading: Mobile surveillance is its own program
finalCTABody: If you are buying $50K+ a year of mobile surveillance, buy it direct. If you are an integrator, partner with us at /partners. Either way, get a real quote.

h1: Fixed-Site Mobile Surveillance vs. Fleet, In-Car, and Body-Worn Video
heroSubhead: "Mobile surveillance" returns two completely different markets. One is fixed-site mobile surveillance trailers — solar-autonomous units that move between job sites. The other is in-vehicle and body-worn video for fleets and law enforcement. VDS is in the first market. If you are searching for the second, this page sends you to the right vendors.

heroCTASecondary.label: I need fleet / in-car / body-cam video

body:
## Why this comparison matters

Type "mobile surveillance" into Google and the first page returns vendors selling completely different products. A construction GC and a sheriff's deputy both use the words "mobile surveillance" to describe the thing they need. They need different things.

This page exists to route you to the right category before you spend a quarter chasing the wrong vendor.

## The two markets

| Dimension | Fixed-Site Mobile Surveillance | Fleet / In-Car / Body-Worn Video |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Solar-autonomous surveillance trailers and pole-mounted units that deploy to a site for weeks or months | Video cameras mounted in vehicles or worn by personnel that record continuously while the asset is in motion |
| Where it lives | At a site — construction yard, lay-down area, utility substation, retail parking, remote property | Inside or on a vehicle or person — patrol car, transit bus, delivery truck, officer's chest |
| Mobility model | Redeployable between sites; static while on-site | Always moving with the vehicle or person |
| Power model | Solar autonomous, optional grid | Vehicle 12V or worn battery |
| Primary buyer | Construction, utility, retail, municipal, energy, federal sites | Law enforcement, transit, public works fleets, delivery, trucking |
| Primary use case | Theft deterrence, perimeter monitoring, post-incident evidence, remote site oversight | Officer accountability, fleet incident review, body-worn evidence chain, dashcam claims defense |
| Storage and chain of custody | Cloud-first, immutable audit log, RBAC, MFA | DEMS-style chain of custody, court-admissible export, prosecutor handoff |
| 24/7 monitoring | Often — VDS SOC runs this | Rarely — assets are mobile and operator-led |
| AI focus | LPR, person/vehicle/intrusion at perimeter | Driver behavior, collision detection, body-cam event flags |
| Procurement model | Rental or purchase per site / per unit | Per-vehicle or per-officer license, often multi-year contract |

## Leading vendors in fleet / in-car / body-worn video

VDS does not sell in this market. If you got here looking for in-car or body-cam video, here are the named vendors most US buyers shortlist:

- **Axon** — The dominant US body-worn camera vendor. Integrated with Axon Evidence (cloud DEMS) and Taser. Strong law enforcement footprint.
- **Apollo Video Technology** — Mobile DVR systems for transit buses, school buses, paratransit, and rail. Strong public-transit references.
- **Safety Vision** — Mobile video for school buses, transit, law enforcement vehicles, and commercial fleets. Long US history.
- **AngelTrax** — School bus and pupil transportation video systems. Strong K-12 references.
- **Digital Ally** — In-car video and body cameras for law enforcement. Publicly traded.
- **Utility** — In-car and body-worn video with integrated wireless upload and cloud DEMS.
- **TSI Video** (Transit Safety Inc.) — Transit and commercial fleet mobile video.

This is not a ranking and it is not exhaustive. It is a starting shortlist so you can route yourself out of the fixed-site mobile surveillance category and into the right RFP.

## Leading vendors in fixed-site mobile surveillance

If you got here looking for solar-autonomous surveillance trailers, the shortlist is on /compare/top-mobile-surveillance-companies. The vendors are LVT, ECAM, Flock Safety, WCCTV, Pro-Vigil, Verkada, Spot AI, Deploy Surveillance, GoView, and VDS.

## How to tell which market you need

Answer these three questions:

1. **Does the camera need to move continuously with a vehicle or person?**
   - Yes → fleet / in-car / body-worn. Talk to Axon, Apollo, Safety Vision, AngelTrax, Digital Ally, Utility, or TSI Video.
   - No → fixed-site mobile surveillance. Talk to VDS.

2. **Will the camera sit at a fixed location for weeks or months, then redeploy to a new site?**
   - Yes → fixed-site mobile surveillance. This is VDS.
   - No → not VDS.

3. **Is your primary use case officer accountability, court-admissible body-cam evidence, or fleet driver behavior?**
   - Yes → fleet / in-car / body-worn.
   - No, your use case is theft deterrence, perimeter monitoring, and remote site oversight → fixed-site mobile surveillance.

## Where the two markets sometimes overlap

A utility operator might use VDS at a substation perimeter AND Apollo Video on their service trucks. A municipality might run Flock Safety ALPR poles in city neighborhoods AND Axon body cameras on the patrol force. The two markets serve adjacent buyers and sometimes the same buyer for different jobs.

The key is that the procurement, RFP language, evaluation criteria, and vendor lists are different. Buying body-worn cameras from a mobile surveillance trailer vendor is a category error. Buying mobile surveillance trailers from a body-cam vendor is also a category error.

## Where VDS wins inside fixed-site mobile surveillance

500+ deployments across 30+ states. Three product lines (Sky Guard MSU, Swift Deploy, Boundary Guard Pro). AI VisionStream — camera-agnostic ONVIF/RTSP, 95%+ LPR at sub-3-second match. 24/7 in-house US SOC with sub-60-second escalation and 97% false-alarm reduction. NDAA Section 889 compliant. US AWS-only data residency. Published pricing from $1,500/mo (Swift Deploy) and from $38,000 purchase (Sky Guard).

Hero case study: $28M Mid-Atlantic GC — 73% theft reduction, $0 insurance claims, $340,800 saved in 12 months.

faq.q: Does VDS sell body-worn cameras?
faq.a: No. VDS does not make body-worn cameras. For body-worn cameras, look at Axon, Digital Ally, or Utility.

faq.q: Does VDS make in-car police cameras?
faq.a: No. For in-car law enforcement video, look at Digital Ally, Utility, or Axon.

faq.q: Can VDS provide cameras for school buses or transit fleets?
faq.a: No. For school bus, transit, or fleet video, look at Apollo Video Technology, Safety Vision, or AngelTrax.

faq.q: Why do these markets both call themselves "mobile surveillance"?
faq.a: Historical naming. The fixed-site mobile surveillance category emerged from camera trailers that move between sites. The fleet / in-car category emerged from cameras mounted on moving assets. Both use "mobile." Procurement teams should specify "mobile surveillance trailer" or "fleet / body-worn video" to disambiguate.

faq.a: /compare/top-mobile-surveillance-companies has a ranked matrix of the 10 leading US fixed-site mobile surveillance operators.

finalCTAHeading: You are in the right place if your camera does not move
finalCTABody: If your use case is a fixed site — construction yard, utility substation, retail lot, municipal property — VDS is the right vendor. If it is a vehicle or a person, the named vendors above are where to start.
